slides.title: The question: cleaner steel for German manufacturing
slides.key_message: We ask how EU ETS and CBAM together shape the move to cleaner steel for German manufacturing, using descriptive evidence and no causal claim.
slides.visual: Title card with the question and a three-block roadmap ribbon CH1 Policy -> CH2 Economic effects -> CH3 Conclusion and suggestion (this ribbon repeats thinly on every slide). Under CH2, the 11 required variables as greyed chips: X, M, NX, BOP, Q, P, GDP, Tax, C, I, G (they light up on S5-S10). Three stat tiles, each with its definition printed: '19.4% of German total GVA is manufacturing, 2025 (not a GDP share)' [U22]; '26% of EU sold industrial production is German, 2025 (production value, PRODCOM, not GDP)' [U26]; '34.1 Mt German crude steel, 2025' [Dataset A, S13]. Badge strip: 'Germany | iron and steel feeding manufacturing | descriptive method: no DiD, policy dates are annotations not proof'.
speaker_points: Question: how do EU ETS and CBAM together influence the long-term move to cleaner steel supply for German manufacturing, and which opportunities and adjustment costs appear?

Why Germany and steel: manufacturing is 19.4% of German value added (2025) and Germany holds 26% of EU sold industrial production, a production share, not GDP. CBAM is EU-wide law and Germany applies the common framework [S1][S2].
Method: descriptive graphs, course theory and dated company cases. No regression; policy dates are annotations, not proof of cause.
Roadmap: CH1 the policies, CH2 the effects on X, M, NX, BOP, Q, P, GDP, tax, C, I and G, CH3 keep, change or drop.

slides.title: Why price carbon: emissions are a cost society bears
slides.key_message: Steelmaking emissions cost society more than the producer pays; a carbon price makes producers face that cost, which is the logic of the EU ETS.
slides.visual: THEORY DIAGRAM 1 of 2: Fig. 1 = sources/images/base-doc-fig-01.png reused unchanged (negative production externality: demand D, private marginal cost PMC, social cost SMC = PMC + 20, market Q = 50 versus social optimum Q = 40, shaded avoidable-loss triangle; its footer 'SIMULATION | Invented values for theory; not observed German data' stays). Beside it a three-box before / during / latest strip of real facts. BEFORE: 'pre-ETS window 1995-2004; ETS Directive adopted 2003'. DURING: '2005 launch; pilot 2005-07 with mostly free allocation and oversupply, not a uniform charge' [U1]. LATEST: 'covered power + industry emissions about 50% below 2005 in 2024: EU aggregate, power-led, not Germany-steel, not CBAM' [U29]. Caption: 'Short-run static, one point in time; carbon cost set equal to damage by assumption'. Text fallback if the lecturer rejects the graph: a two-line wedge statement plus the same strip.
speaker_points: Course link, negative production externality [G1]: social marginal cost sits above private, so the unpriced market produces Q = 50 where the social optimum is 40. The numbers are invented.
A carbon cost makes the producer pay that gap. ETS caps covered emissions; it is not a steel-output quota [G4]. We do not claim the real ETS price equals the damage.

Before, during, latest: the observation window starts pre-ETS; in 2005 the pilot used mostly free allocation, so it was not a sudden uniform charge [U1]; by 2024 covered emissions were about 50% below 2005, an EU aggregate led by power [U29].

slides.title: Two tools, one logic: ETS inside, CBAM at the border
slides.key_message: ETS prices emissions inside the EU and CBAM applies the same carbon-cost comparison to covered imports by embedded emissions, so it is neither a ban nor a flat tariff.
slides.visual: Two-column comparison table, 5 rows, at most about 8 words per cell, with an arrow between the headers 'same carbon-cost logic'. Headers: 'EU ETS (inside the EU)' | 'CBAM (at the border)'. Rows: What: 'Declining cap, tradable allowances' | 'Carbon cost on covered imports, by embedded emissions'. Who surrenders: 'Installations surrender allowances' | 'Authorised declarant surrenders certificates'. Price: 'Allowance auction price' | 'Certificate price follows ETS auctions'. Start: '2005 (pilot, mostly free allocation)' | 'Reporting Oct 2023; definitive 1 Jan 2026'. Not: 'Not a uniform charge in 2005' | 'Not a ban, not buy-European, not a % of invoice value'. Footer chip: 'Cleaner supplier -> smaller bill (assumed example in backup A3)'.
speaker_points: ETS: a declining cap and tradable allowances; installations surrender allowances. Free allocation lowers the net cost but is not an exemption from monitoring and surrender [U1][U2].

CBAM: the authorised declarant surrenders certificates for embedded emissions, net of free-allocation adjustments and any recognised foreign carbon price; certificate prices follow ETS auctions [U3][U5].
So a cleaner supplier faces a smaller bill, and it is not a fixed percentage of import value; the assumed worked example is in backup.
Germany applies the EU rules and sets no German tariff [S1][S2]. Coverage by customs code (mostly Chapter 72, scrap excluded) and the 50-tonne importer threshold are in backup A4.

slides.key_message: Carbon pricing arrived in stages and CBAM's cash payments start in 2027, so all our output and trade data end in 2025, before any paid CBAM charge.
slides.visual: Two-lane horizontal timeline 1995-2034, at most 8 labelled events in lane 1. Lane 1 'Climate policy': 2005 ETS launch (pilot 2005-07; phases 2008-12, 2013-20, 2021 onward) [U1]; 14 Jul 2021 CBAM proposed [S3]; 1 Oct 2023 reporting starts, no payments [U3][S7]; 1 Jan 2026 definitive regime [S6]; 1 Feb 2027 certificate sales begin; 30 Sep 2027 first surrender [U35][S5]; 2034 phase-in complete [S9]. Lane 2 'Separate trade measure, not CBAM': steel quota framework adopted 8 Jun 2026, applied 1 Jul 2026, 47% below 2024 safeguard quotas [U6][U8]; footnote 'Russia sanctions are another separate factor' [U33]. One-line strip: 'CBAM factor 97.5% (2026) -> 0% (2034), benchmark-based, not a % of each shipment's emissions' [S9][S10]. Thin data-window bar: 'manufacturing 1995-2025; extra-EU Ch. 72 imports 1999-2025; both end 2025'.
speaker_points: ETS launched in 2005 as a pilot with mostly free allocation; later phases tightened it [U1]. CBAM was proposed in July 2021, ran as reporting from October 2023 and became definitive on 1 January 2026 [S3][S7][S6].
A 2026 liability and its cash payment are different events: certificate sales begin 1 February 2027 and the first surrender is due 30 September 2027 [U35]. No data we show include a paid CBAM charge.
From 2026 to 2034 CBAM phases in as free allocation is withdrawn; the factor falls from 97.5% to 0% [S9].
The lower lane is a different instrument: the steel quota framework, adopted 8 June 2026 and applied from 1 July, compares with 2024 safeguard quotas [U6][U8].

slides.title: Theory: a carbon cost on imports, but not one-for-one
slides.key_message: A carbon-related import cost narrows the import price advantage, but pass-through is partial and domestic costs rose too, so output and imports respond in an open, short-run way.
slides.visual: THEORY DIAGRAM 2 of 2: REDRAWN Fig. 2 (the original full-pass-through figure is not shown). Qualitative axes 'Price' and 'Quantity of steel', no numbers; footer 'ILLUSTRATIVE | qualitative, not observed German data'. Curves: demand D; domestic supply S and a second curve S' shifted UP (ETS, energy and capital cost rise); flat import-price line P_M0 rising to P_M1 with a short arrow labelled 'less than the full carbon cost (partial pass-through)'. Movement along curves and the shift of S are marked differently. Annotations: price paid up; quantity demanded down; domestic output ambiguous; import gap not guaranteed to fall. Below, a BEFORE / DURING / AFTER strip with real facts: BEFORE: 'industrial electricity 5.92 ct/kWh (2020), peak 35.70 (2022), 16.77 (2024)' [BaseNotes-3, SMARD; verify at source]. DURING (reporting Oct 2023-Dec 2025, no payments): 'extra-EU Ch. 72 imports 2,089 -> 1,464 kt (2023 -> 2025)' [U24]. AFTER (2026+): 'certificate EUR 75.36 / 75.28 / 82.32 per tCO2e, Q1-Q3 2026' [Dataset E]; 'no 2026 trade data; first payments 2027; no after-effect claim' [U35]. Chips lit: M, Q, P. Text fallback if the lecturer rejects the graph: a mechanism box with the same strip.
speaker_points: Static short run. A carbon cost lifts imported steel's landed price, but by less than the full charge, because exporters and importers absorb part.
Domestic supply also shifts up with ETS, energy and capital costs. So domestic output and imports are ambiguous, and total imports need not fall if sourcing moves within the EU.

Before: electricity peaked at 35.70 ct/kWh in 2022. During reporting, with no payments due, extra-EU imports fell from 2,089 to 1,464 thousand tonnes, so this is not a payment effect; anticipation would need its own evidence. After: 2026 prices exist, payments start in 2027, so no after-effect claim.

slides.title: German manufacturing, 1995-2025
slides.key_message: Real manufacturing output grew through the ETS launch, fell sharply in 2009 and 2020 and has softened since 2022; a graph alone cannot separate policy from energy, demand and COVID.
slides.visual: Two stacked line panels on a shared 1995-2025 x-axis, never on one y-axis. Panel A: real GVA, chain-linked volume index, 2020 = 100 [U22]. Panel B: production index, annual unadjusted, 2021 = 100 [U23]. Dashed markers at 2005 (ETS launch) and Oct 2023 (CBAM reporting); right-edge label '2026 definitive regime (beyond data)'; light bands on 2009 and 2020. Side tile (not plotted): 'Manufacturing share of total GVA 22.3% (1995) -> 19.4% (2025); EU27 15.9% (2024); a share of value added, not of GDP' [U22]. Footnote: '2023-25 GVA provisional'. Footer: 'Does not show: an ETS or CBAM effect, or no effect. Backup A1.' Chips lit: Q, GDP.
speaker_points: Two series on two panels with two base years; the share tile is value added, not GDP.
Around the 2005 launch both series rose, so no launch-year shock; the pilot was mostly free allocation, so this is an annotation, not an effect.
The deepest falls are 2009 (GVA index about 93 to 74) and 2020; since 2022 production slipped from about 100 to 93. The share of value added eased from 22.3% to 19.4%.
A stable or falling aggregate cannot prove or rule out a policy effect; plant-level change hides inside averages.

slides.key_message: Direct extra-EU Chapter 72 imports peaked at 6,291 kt in 2007 and have fallen every year since 2021 to a series low of 1,464 kt in 2025, while overlapping events prevent reading this as a policy effect.
slides.visual: Two stacked panels on a shared 1999-2025 axis. Panel A: net mass, thousand tonnes (bars) [U24]. Panel B: import value, EUR million, nominal (line) [U24]. Text-only event labels: 2005 ETS launch; 2008-09 financial crisis; 2020 COVID; 2022 energy and war shock; Oct 2023 CBAM reporting. speaker_points: Tonnes and euros sit on separate panels because they move differently: unit value was EUR 736 per tonne in 2019, 1,176 in 2022 and 1,087 in 2025, a product-mix measure.

Imports rose after the 2005 launch to the 2007 peak, so we do not claim ETS cut imports. Since 2021 tonnes fell every year; the 2008-09 crisis, COVID, the 2022 energy and war shock, Russia sanctions and quotas all overlap.
During the reporting years 2023-25 tonnes fell from 2,089 to 1,464 thousand before any payment, so no payment effect can be read from them.
Boundary: steel cleared in another EU state and then sent to Germany is not counted, so this is not total German use of non-EU steel.

slides.section: CH2 Economic effects: data (Member B's added steel exports and NX; 'chap 4.2')
slides.title: Steel exports and NX: what we can and cannot show
slides.key_message: On an all-partner physical basis the steel balance moved from -1.2 Mt (2017) to +4.1 Mt (2024) while imports fell faster than exports; the matched extra-EU export series is not in hand, so we draw no competitiveness verdict.
slides.visual: One chart: two lines, exports 27.3 -> 22.9 Mt and imports 28.5 -> 18.8 Mt, 2017-2024, 'steel mill products, ALL partners incl. intra-EU, million tonnes, rounded' [Dataset B]. Directly under the x-axis a one-row strip 'approximate balance X - M, derived from rounded values (Mt): -1.2, -1.6, +0.3, +1.4, -0.4, +0.4, +3.0, +4.1'. Small separate tile on its own axis: 'Crude steel output 43.3 -> 37.2 Mt (2017 -> 2024): a different measure' [Dataset A]. One-line gap box: 'Not shown: matched extra-EU Chapter 72 exports (Comext flow 2, 1999-2025), so no extra-EU NX; not comparable in level with slide 7'. Scope badge: 'Not the CBAM base; not national-accounts NX (goods and services, EUR)'. Chips lit: X, M, NX; BOP footnote 'goods trade is one part of the current account'. Footer: 'Does not show: competitiveness. Backup A6.'
speaker_points: Member B's point: imports alone say nothing about competitiveness, so we add exports. NX is X minus M; here it means steel only, in tonnes.

What we have: all-partner steel mill products. Exports fell from 27.3 to 22.9 million tonnes and imports from 28.5 to 18.8, so the approximate balance rose from -1.2 to +4.1 Mt. It is derived from rounded values and not monotonic: 2021 was -0.4.

Why no verdict: both flows and crude steel output (43.3 to 37.2 Mt) fell, so a bigger tonnage surplus can come from weak home demand. It is also a different universe from slide 7, so we never subtract one series from the other.
What is missing: matched extra-EU exports and euro values. We make no claim about extra-EU NX or Germany's goods-and-services NX, and the goods balance is not the balance of payments.

speaker_points: Three cases, each with an opportunity and a limit. Keep the words exact: buyer versus producer, MoU versus contract versus delivery.
VW-Thyssenkrupp is an MoU for supply from 2028. Salzgitter's first plant output is 2027 and its June 2026 hydrogen contract covers about 6.5% of need.
Mercedes and BMW are buyers and Stegra is the producer; Stegra's September 2026 review says more capital is needed, so these are contracts, not deliveries.
Most agreements pre-date paid CBAM; ETS, expected policy, subsidies, buyer targets and technology also matter. This is the investment channel: announced is not spent.

C | Pass-through to final goods may cut spending | 2025 household consumption +1.4% real [Dataset F]. I | Clean-plant investment up, downstream may fall | 2025 fixed investment -0.5% real [Dataset F]; announced is not spent (slide 9). G | Support and infrastructure; subsidies are not all G | 2025 government consumption +1.5% real [Dataset F]. Footer: 'Dataset F rates are one first-estimate vintage (15 Jan 2026), whole-economy context, not CBAM effects. Does not show: any estimated effect. Backup A6.' All 11 chips lit.
speaker_points: Trade block: steel exports and imports are shown and NX is derived for steel only; goods trade is one part of the balance of payments, which stays separate (2025 current-account surplus about EUR 203 billion, not a steel effect).
Market block: tonnes are down and unit values up but mix-affected; services respond only indirectly through engineering, verification and logistics, and we have no series for them.
Macro block: GDP = C + I + G + NX is accounting. The 2025 growth rates (GDP +0.2%, consumption +1.4%, investment -0.5%, government +1.5%) are national context from one vintage, not policy effects.
Tax: not yet observable. Certificate sales start in February 2027, and ETS or CBAM receipts are not automatically German tax revenue or government spending.

slides.section: CH2 Economic effects: costs, conditions and limits (Member B 2.6)
slides.title: Costs and conditions: what has to go right
slides.key_message: Cleaner steel is still a premium or a gap in many settings, so any long-term benefit is conditional on clean power and hydrogen, finance, delivery and regional adjustment.
slides.visual: Three cards under 'What has to go right', plus a banner and a footer line. Card 1 'Price gap': 'IEA: cost gaps often remain even with policy support' [U20] (chip: published analysis); 'Salzgitter: new energy inputs currently dearer than coal' [U12]. Card 2 'Capital and delivery': 'Stegra needs additional capital to complete Boden (30 Sep 2026)' [U16]; 'EWE hydrogen covers about 6.5% of SALCOS need' [U13]. Card 3 'People and regions': 'Thyssenkrupp plan, 25 Nov 2024: about 5,000 job reductions by 2030 + about 6,000 transferred or sold; not 11,000 dismissals; pre-dates definitive CBAM' [U9]. Banner: 'We do not say green steel is cheaper.' Footer: 'Also at work: energy prices, COVID, Russia sanctions, the separate steel quota, ETS free-allocation changes' [U33][U6]; 'Remaining high-carbon supply and wider sectors: backup A8, A12.'
speaker_points: We do not claim green steel is cheaper: the IEA finds cost gaps often remain even with policy support, and Salzgitter says its new energy inputs cost more than coal today.
Projects need money: Stegra says it needs more capital, and the EWE contract covers about 6.5% of SALCOS hydrogen need.
Adjustment is uneven: Thyssenkrupp's 2024 plan is about 5,000 cuts plus about 6,000 transfers or sales by 2030, not 11,000 dismissals, and it pre-dates definitive CBAM. Costs are not only downstream.
Energy prices, COVID, sanctions, the steel quota and free-allocation changes overlap, so any benefit stays conditional on clean power, hydrogen, finance and verified data.

slides.title: Conclusion: can strengthen, if conditions hold
slides.key_message: The evidence is consistent with ETS and CBAM supporting a move to cleaner steel, but a measured net German gain, cost parity and delivered tonnes are not shown.
slides.visual: Verdict banner: 'EU ETS + CBAM can strengthen the long-term move to cleaner steel; the net German benefit is unmeasured and conditional.' Three columns with per-item chips. CONSISTENT WITH: carbon-cost comparison now includes embedded emissions [U3] (Policy rule); dated buyer and producer commitments 2021-26 [U10][U12][U13][U14][U15][U16] (Company announcement); covered ETS emissions about 50% below 2005 in 2024, EU aggregate, power-led [U29] (Observed); OECD: about 10% emissions cut 2005-12, no measured harm to regulated firms, earlier period [U30] (Published research). NOT SHOWN: causal size of any effect; net German GDP or welfare gain (scenario studies: small, assumption-sensitive [S19], Model-based); green steel cheaper; delivered tonnes; paid-CBAM effects (first payments 2027); extra-EU steel NX. CONDITIONAL ON: affordable clean power and hydrogen; finance; verified emissions data; workable administration [U12][U20]. Footer: 'Verdict = team judgement drawn from descriptive evidence, not a measured finding.'
speaker_points: Answer: yes in direction, conditionally. The carbon-cost comparison now includes emissions, buyers and producers have dated plans, and covered EU ETS emissions were about 50% below 2005 in 2024, an EU aggregate led by power [U29].
Earlier research on the first ETS years found about 10% emissions cuts without measured harm to regulated firms [U30]. Neither result is about CBAM or German steel.
Not shown: causal size, a net German GDP gain, cost parity, delivered tonnes and paid-CBAM effects. Scenario studies find small, assumption-sensitive GDP effects [S19].
So our title says 'can strengthen', conditional on clean power and hydrogen, finance, verified data and workable administration.

slides.title: Suggestion: keep the framework, change the delivery
slides.key_message: Keep a predictable ETS plus CBAM framework, improve how it is delivered, and reconsider only if monitoring shows leakage, losses that exceed benefits, or no verified fall in emissions.
slides.visual: Three-column table KEEP | CHANGE | DROP or RECONSIDER IF. KEEP: 'Predictable ETS + CBAM framework with the legislated phase-in to 2034' [S9]; 'Climate-policy design kept separate from trade-defence decisions such as the steel quota' [U6]. CHANGE (5 short items): '1 Emissions data and verification, transparent default values' [S11]; '2 Clean power, hydrogen and scrap infrastructure with evaluated support'; '3 Proportionate compliance: check the 50-tonne threshold (Sep 2026 assessment: exempts 0.87% of embedded emissions)' [S23]; '4 Monitor downstream users before any extension (still a proposal; Parliament amendments 15 Sep 2026 referred to negotiation)' [U32][S24]; '5 Retraining and regional adjustment support' [U9]. DROP OR RECONSIDER IF: 'Nothing to drop now. Reconsider if monitoring shows leakage or resource shuffling; downstream and regional losses exceed benefits; no verified fall in emissions per tonne.' Bottom strip: 'Monitor: physical trade | input prices | domestic value added | realised investment | verified emissions per tonne | administration cost. Refresh points: Feb 2027 sales, 30 Sep 2027 surrender.' Footer: 'Team judgement, not a measured finding.'
speaker_points: Keep: investment decisions need a predictable signal, so we would keep ETS plus CBAM and the legislated phase-in to 2034 [S9].

Change the delivery: better emissions data and verification [S11]; clean power, hydrogen and scrap infrastructure, because border protection alone does not make a plant cleaner; proportionate compliance, noting the September 2026 assessment that the 50-tonne threshold exempts 0.87% of embedded emissions [S23].
Watch downstream firms before any extension, which is still only a proposal [U32], and support retraining and regional adjustment, since stable aggregates can hide plant-level losses [U9].
Drop: nothing now, but we name the triggers that would reopen the question, and we keep climate design apart from trade-defence decisions such as the steel quota.

appendix_slides.title: A1. Fast answers: panel questions on one page
appendix_slides.content: Why start before 2005 (manufacturing 1995, imports 1999)? Context before domestic carbon pricing; an illustration, not an evaluation. Why no DiD? The assignment explains trade mechanisms; a credible causal design needs its own design and data, and ETS exemptions complicate comparison groups. Did CBAM force the contracts? Several pre-date 2026; ETS, expected policy, subsidies, buyer targets and technology also matter. Is DRI always fossil-free? No, gas can be used first. Can China supply cleaner steel? Judge installation and route, not nationality. Are all negative effects downstream? No: producers, regions, importers, energy and logistics users can bear costs. Has CBAM's German GDP effect been shown to be zero? No; this research does not estimate it. Finland-to-Germany steel? Intra-EU, so no new border charge; footprint is a separate question. Why Germany if CBAM is EU-wide? Implementation and incidence case; Germany applies the common framework. Is CBAM a fixed tariff? No: it depends on embedded emissions and adjustments. Does non-EU mean every origin pays? No: exempt origins and the 50-tonne importer threshold. Does a fall in imports prove success? No; test global emissions, welfare, downstream costs and resource shuffling. Why not say GDP rises because M falls? GDP = C + I + G + NX is an identity; domestic value added matters. Does the 2.5% phase-in mean 2.5% of emissions is charged? No; it is benchmark-based. Can 2024-25 data prove a 2026 effect? No; they give baseline conditions, and any anticipation effect needs its own evidence. Protectionism or WTO-compatible? GATT Article XX allows environmental exceptions under conditions; EU statements say CBAM is designed to comply, which is not a WTO ruling.
appendix_slides.answers_question: The standard defence questions (update tab section 9 and base 3.3) with one-line answers and the slide or backup page that holds the evidence.

appendix_slides.title: A2. Claims we corrected, and what we say instead
appendix_slides.content: 'Manufacturing GDP barely changed, so CBAM had no effect': the screenshot has no clear unit and appears to show a rate; a stable aggregate cannot identify an effect; use GVA and production series [U22][U23]. '14% GDP share, 26% weight': use 19.4% of German total GVA in 2025 (19.9% in 2024; EU27 15.9%) [U22]; 26% is Germany's 2025 share of EU sold industrial production, EU total about EUR 6.1 trillion, not GDP [U26]. '5.5 million workers = 20.8% of the workforce': use national-accounts Section C employment 7.490 m (2023), 7.415 m (2024), 7.262 m (2025) [U28]; the 20.8% has no verified denominator; EU structural statistics (about 30.2 m, 18.5% of the business economy) are a different universe [U27]. 'CBAM cut tariff-free quotas by 47%': the 47% belongs to the separate steel quota framework versus 2024 safeguard quotas, applied from 1 Jul 2026 [U6][U8]. 'CBAM caused 11,000 dismissals': the 25 Nov 2024 plan is about 5,000 cuts plus about 6,000 transfers or sales and pre-dates the definitive regime [U9]. 'Green steel is already cheaper': a premium or gap remains in many settings [U19][U20]. 'Contracts show all automotive steel is hydrogen': separate buyer from producer, MoU from contract, target from delivered tonnes, original from revised dates [U10][U14][U15][U16]. Chat wording also corrected: Mercedes is the buyer, not the plant operator; BMW's agreement does not replace all BMW steel; bluemint is a product family and recycled bluemint is not hydrogen DRI [U11]; Outokumpu reports 97% recycled material content in 2025, not '90% scrap' [U18]. Not used (not validated): 67 distressed regions, 26 German regions, EUR 50 bn outsourcing loss, EUR 7 bn subsidies, 1.5% manufacturing rebound.
appendix_slides.answers_question: Earlier material or other groups say X; why does your deck not? (14%, 5.5 m / 20.8%, 47%, 11,000, cheaper green steel, 'GDP barely changed', contracts equal delivery.)

appendix_slides.title: A3. How big is the CBAM charge? Worked example, phase-in and prices
appendix_slides.content: Assumed inputs, not German data: 1,000 t covered steel; embedded emissions e = 2.0 tCO2e/t; benchmark b = 1.0; 2026 factor f = 0.975; correction factor 1; no foreign carbon price. Certificates = quantity x max(0, e - f x b) = 1,000 x (2.0 - 0.975) = 1,025. At the published Q1 2026 price EUR 75.36 that is EUR 77,244, or EUR 77.24 per tonne of steel; with e = 1.2 it is 225 certificates and EUR 16.96 per tonne. Administration and verification costs are extra. Published prices (EUR per tCO2e, not per tonne of steel): Q1 2026 75.36 (7 Apr), Q2 75.28 (6 Jul), Q3 82.32 (5 Oct); Q4 not yet published, so no assumed price [Dataset E][S8]. CBAM factor / complement, %: 2026 97.5 / 2.5; 2027 95.0 / 5.0; 2028 90.0 / 10.0; 2029 77.5 / 22.5; 2030 51.5 / 48.5; 2031 39.0 / 61.0; 2032 26.5 / 73.5; 2033 14.0 / 86.0; 2034 0.0 / 100.0 [S9][S10]. The 2.5% is not 2.5% of each shipment's emissions. Do not use a universal EUR 200-600 per tonne. Show as a two-bar example plus a three-bar price chart, labelled Theoretical-illustrative.
appendix_slides.answers_question: Is CBAM a fixed tariff? What does a certificate cost per tonne of steel? Does a 2.5% phase-in mean only 2.5% of emissions is charged? Does a cleaner supplier really pay less?

appendix_slides.title: A4. What CBAM covers, who is exempt, who pays
appendix_slides.content: Coverage is by customs code: most of Chapter 72 minus specified ferroalloys and scrap (7204); agglomerated iron ore 26011200; Chapter 73 headings 7301-7311, 7318 and 7326 (not all of Chapter 73) [S4]. Exempt origins: Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland and Annex III territories; EU-to-EU purchases trigger no border charge [S4]. 50-tonne importer threshold: per importer per calendar year, aggregated across covered goods, all-or-nothing once exceeded [S5]. The 2025 reform was expected to exempt about 90% of importers while keeping about 99% of covered emissions (EU framework, not German shares) [S7]; the Sep 2026 assessment puts the exemption at 0.87% of embedded emissions [S23]. Legal payer: the authorised declarant; the economic burden can be shared by contract; German enforcement by DEHSt at UBA [S6][S7]. Steel uses direct emissions within production boundaries, not a full life-cycle footprint [S7][S10][U34]. Registry context: about 108 Mt of EU CBAM iron-and-steel imports over Q4 2023-Q2 2025 and about 15,000 iron-and-steel reports to the German authority (reports are not companies; EU-wide tonnage; rounded) [S21].
appendix_slides.answers_question: What exactly is covered? Does 'non-EU' mean every origin is charged? Who pays? Why Germany if CBAM is EU-wide? What is the 50-tonne rule?

appendix_slides.title: A5. The steel quota measure, sanctions and dumping are not CBAM
appendix_slides.content: Steel tariff-rate quota framework: Council agreement 13 Apr 2026, adopted 8 Jun 2026, applied from 1 Jul 2026; 47% lower than the 2024 safeguard quotas; replaces the safeguard and addresses global overcapacity [U6][U8]. The update tab lists 18.3 Mt a year and a 50% out-of-quota duty for the framework; check the U7 wording on which quota the 18.3 Mt describes before showing it. Carbon leakage and overcapacity are distinct problems; CBAM's stated rationale is leakage prevention. Dumping has a trade-law meaning and cannot be inferred from a low price; carbon intensity does not determine grade. Russian iron and steel trade is separately affected by sanctions and origin restrictions, so a fall in Russian supply cannot be assigned to CBAM or to a hydrogen switch [U33]. Chinese suppliers are heterogeneous: do not call all Chinese steel low grade or all imports dirty. Safeguards, quotas, anti-dumping, sanctions, subsidies and energy policy are separate instruments that may hit the same market. Member D's priority 2 (the quota adjustment, 'not required') is answered only here.
appendix_slides.answers_question: Is the 47% quota cut part of CBAM? Isn't this really Chinese dumping? Did CBAM cut Russian supply? Can China supply cleaner steel?

appendix_slides.title: A6. NX and BOP: definitions, full Dataset B, and the export-data pull
appendix_slides.content: NX in GDP is goods and services exports minus imports in value; Dataset B is physical tonnes of steel mill products, all partners incl. intra-EU, rounded to 0.1 Mt [S12]. Exports (Mt) 2017-2024: 27.3, 26.4, 24.8, 22.1, 24.6, 23.2, 23.0, 22.9. Imports: 28.5, 28.0, 24.5, 20.7, 25.0, 22.8, 20.0, 18.8. Approximate balance X - M: -1.2, -1.6, +0.3, +1.4, -0.4, +0.4, +3.0, +4.1. Crude steel 2017-2025: 43.3, 42.4, 39.6, 35.7, 40.2, 36.9, 35.4, 37.2, 34.1 [Dataset A]. A steel-only improvement can coexist with a weaker total surplus. Goods trade is one part of the current account; BOP also has capital and financial accounts; Germany shares the euro, so a steel balance does not set a German exchange rate [S18]. 2025 context: merchandise exports EUR 1,562.9 bn, imports EUR 1,362.5 bn, surplus EUR 200.4 bn [S17]; current-account surplus about EUR 203 bn [S18]; real exports -0.3%, imports +3.6% [Dataset F]. To close the gap: Comext DS-045409, reporter DE, partner EXT_EU27_2020, flow 2 (exports), product 72, freq A, VALUE_IN_EUROS and QUANTITY_IN_100KG, 1999-2025; tonnes = 100-kg units / 10, thousand tonnes / 1,000, EUR million / 1,000,000; missing stays missing [U24][U25]. Apparent consumption = production + imports - exports needs a separate production source on a matched boundary; do not mix crude steel with mill products.
appendix_slides.answers_question: Where is the extra-EU steel export and NX series? Does a positive steel balance mean competitiveness improved? How do steel NX, GDP and BOP relate?

appendix_slides.title: A7. Reading the import series: events, unit values, hot-rolled detail
appendix_slides.content: Direct extra-EU Chapter 72 imports [U24], kt (value EUR m): 2004 3,906.31 (2,476.91); 2005 4,744.27 (3,363.02); 2007 6,290.77 (5,660.36); 2009 3,503.05 (2,465.29); 2018 4,666.28 (3,345.39); 2020 2,833.77 (1,862.49); 2021 3,337.39 (2,762.68); 2022 2,697.17 (3,171.16); 2023 2,088.99 (2,107.38); 2024 1,954.63 (1,876.92); 2025 1,463.59 (1,590.95). Unit value EUR/t 2019-2025: 735.94, 657.25, 827.80, 1,175.74, 1,008.80, 960.24, 1,087.02, a product-mix indicator [Dataset C]. Covered subset 7208 hot-rolled [Dataset D]: 91.12 kt (2019) to 32.72 kt (2025); unit value 693.45 to 1,009.32 EUR/t with a 1,380.62 peak in 2022; do not extrapolate to all steel. Shock list to name aloud: ETS 2005, financial crisis 2008-09, COVID 2020, energy and war 2022, CBAM reporting Oct 2023, Russia sanctions, quotas. Imports rose after the 2005 launch, consistent with mostly free allocation and strong demand; no ETS import effect is claimed. Direct imports omit non-EU steel first cleared elsewhere in the EU, and the fixed EXT_EU27_2020 composition is not the historical EU. 1995-1998 and 2026 returned no values and are not filled with zero.
appendix_slides.answers_question: Why did imports rise after 2005? Did CBAM cut imports? Why did unit values spike in 2022? Is Chapter 72 the CBAM base? What happened to hot-rolled coil?

appendix_slides.title: A8. What still enters from outside the EU, and what 'cleaner' means
appendix_slides.content: Direct extra-EU imports into Germany, 2025, thousand tonnes / EUR million [U24]: 7207 semi-finished 175.16 / 88.64; 7208 hot-rolled flat 32.72 / 33.03; 7209 cold-rolled flat 1.57 / 1.90; 7210 coated flat 51.52 / 59.73; 7219 stainless flat 9.94 / 35.03; 7304 seamless tubes 87.38 / 233.39; 7306 welded tubes 159.44 / 232.36; 26011200 agglomerated iron ore 2,035.12 / 238.23. Selected non-overlapping profiles, not a CBAM total. A customs code identifies the product, not the furnace route, grid mix or hydrogen source, so these profiles still enter with an unknown footprint; do not infer carbon from origin or price. Routes [U21][U10][U12]: blast furnace + basic oxygen (coal and coke, usually most emissions-intensive); scrap-based EAF (cleaner, depends on electricity and scrap quality, not zero); natural-gas DRI + EAF (lower than coal, still fossil); hydrogen DRI (advantage depends on genuinely low-emission hydrogen and power); stainless and alloy grades (high recycled content does not make them interchangeable with automotive flat carbon steel). Procurement evidence checklist: code and grade; origin and installation; route; scrap or DRI share; hydrogen and power source; measured emissions with boundary and unit; verification; delivery year and volume; price or premium [U34]. 2025 German crude steel was 69.4% oxygen-process and 30.6% electric-process, a context indicator only [S22].
appendix_slides.answers_question: Which materials still arrive from outside the EU? Does continued import mean an unchanged footprint? Is DRI always fossil-free? What would count as evidence that supply is cleaner?

appendix_slides.title: A9. Is green steel cheaper? Price and alternatives (Member D priority 1)
appendix_slides.content: Answer: cost parity is not shown; a premium or gap remains in many settings and future competitiveness is conditional [U19][U20][U12]. Provisional figures from BaseNotes-2 (analyst or secondary estimates, not a price series; attach IDs before use): scrap-EAF premium about EUR 96/t (HSBC estimate); green primary steel premium about EUR 100-200/t in 2025 (Fastmarkets-reported) and EUR 124-223/t estimated for 2026 (DIW); World Economic Forum: under 1% of global steel meets net-zero thresholds, business-to-business premium about 40%. Alternatives for carmakers: scrap-EAF is the most cost-competitive lower-carbon route but limited by scrap quality and sorting; post-consumer secondary steel was 11.3% of steel in new ICE vehicles and 5.3% in EVs; average aluminium per EU and UK car 174 kg (2019) to 205 kg (2022); BEV 283 kg versus 169 kg for ICE-only (2022); low-carbon aluminium differential about USD 0-20/t for most of 2025; composites remain component-specific. Buyer willingness to pay differs by population: a 2024 Ramboll, Climate Group and IEA survey found more than half of buyers would pay up to a 25% premium, while the Commission estimates 16% of steel buyers; quote with populations. Unreconciled before use: scrap import price EUR 305/t (HS 720449, 2025) versus EUR 382/t (HS 7204 aggregate, 2025), and a garbled 'US250/t' aluminium line.
appendix_slides.answers_question: Is green steel cheaper than other materials or EU import prices? What are the practical alternatives? Why do firms not simply switch?

appendix_slides.title: A10. Domestic production-cost data (Member D data request 3)
appendix_slides.content: All figures are provisional BaseNotes-3 values (SMARD, Eionet/EEX, Clean Hydrogen Observatory, S&P, WV Stahl, DIW); verify at source and attach IDs before moving any to a main slide. Industrial electricity, companies without reductions, ct/kWh: 2020 5.92; 2021 21.77; 2022 35.70; 2023 19.63; 2024 16.77; Jan 2025 17.99; Jan-Sep 2025 about 16 (nearly triple 2020 in 2024). Do not use the '+77%' comparison until bases match (eligible-user 10.47 versus the no-concession 5.92 base). EU ETS average allowance price EUR/tCO2e: 83.60 (2023), 64.76 (2024), about 60-80 (2025). Free allocation 2021-2025: initial 2,791.1 m, actual 2,619.6 m, a cut of 171.5 m (about 6.1%). Hydrogen: German renewable (PPA-backed) EUR 10.04/kg on 10 Sep 2025 versus EUR 2.62/kg unabated SMR; European renewable average EUR 6.7/kg in 2024; steel break-even about EUR 2.0/kg. Capital: WV Stahl about EUR 10 bn for one-third of German primary steel and about EUR 30 bn for full conversion; DIW EUR 1.2-2.0 bn per 2 Mt/yr DRI-EAF complex; German projects about EUR 12.5 bn with about EUR 6.9 bn public support for 11.5 Mt/yr. Operating gap: support need about EUR 150/t steel in 2026 rising to about EUR 242/t by the late 2030s (WV Stahl model, a Model-based result). Reading: a structural shift from coal-linked to electricity-, hydrogen- and carbon-linked costs; present conditionally.
appendix_slides.answers_question: Show me the data that German domestic production cost rose. Is it only a downstream problem? How big is the capex and opex gap?

appendix_slides.title: A11. Green support criteria and exemptions (Member D data request 1)
appendix_slides.content: Support is tied to EU or German production assets and verified emissions cuts, not to imported steel as such [BaseNotes-1]. Thyssenkrupp tkH2Steel: up to about EUR 2 bn, a direct grant up to EUR 550 m plus a conditional mechanism up to EUR 1.45 bn for the renewable-hydrogen cost premium in the first ten years, assessed under CEEAG State-aid rules. Salzgitter SALCOS: EUR 1 bn direct grant for a direct-reduction plant, arc furnace and 100 MW electrolyser (about 9,000 t renewable hydrogen a year). Klimaschutzvertraege (carbon contracts for difference): EUR 5 bn German scheme, 15-year contracts, ETS-covered applicants, 60% emissions cut within three years and 90% by project end, open bidding ranked by lowest aid per tonne of CO2 avoided. Imported iron ore, DRI, scrap and hot-rolled steel are not normally subsidised inputs. CBAM has no green-steel exemption: a cleaner import pays less only because its verified embedded emissions are lower; the only broad exemption is the size-based 50-tonne importer threshold [S4][S5]. The production-subsidy diagram (Fig. 3) is not used: it is outside the confirmed title and subsidy sizes exist only as these notes.
appendix_slides.answers_question: Does green support cover imported steel or iron? Is there a green-steel exemption in CBAM? Why is there no subsidy graph?

appendix_slides.title: A12. Jobs, regions, skills and wider sectors
appendix_slides.content: National-accounts manufacturing employment (domestic concept): 7.490 m (2023), 7.415 m (2024), 7.262 m (2025) [U28]; do not state a 2015-2025 range until annual values are pulled. Thyssenkrupp Steel plan, 25 Nov 2024: about 5,000 reductions by 2030 plus about 6,000 transferred or sold, about 40% of a workforce of about 27,000; cites weak competitiveness and cheap imports; pre-dates definitive CBAM [U9]. Later 2025 specification (secondary, BaseNotes-5): IG Metall agreement with no compulsory redundancies, 32.5-hour week, about 8% average income reduction, 1,600 production positions by 2029 plus 3,700 by 2028 = 5,300 directly affected. Skills: shortage of nearly 18,500 qualified workers in metal products and over 16,700 in machinery in 2024 (IW Koeln); automotive transition: about 140,000 further job losses projected in a VDA-commissioned study cited by the Commission. Unemployment rose from 3.2% to 3.5% (end-2023 to end-2024), with services and public sectors offsetting; regional losses (e.g. Duisburg) are the main macro risk. Wider sectors, channels not proven losses: upstream steel regions; automotive, machinery and fabricated metals (input prices, compliance, imported finished goods); construction (steel and cement costs); agriculture via fertiliser (gas and world demand also matter); energy-intensive industries (ETS pass-through); shipping (in ETS from 2024) [U31]; aviation (from 2012). Downstream CBAM extension: Parliament's 15 Sep 2026 amendments were referred to negotiation; the proposed 2028 extension is not the enacted 2026 scope [U32]. Future study: delivered clean-steel tonnes and plant emissions, downstream pass-through, regional retraining, hydrogen and power costs, freight and sourcing, resource shuffling, interaction with quota and sanctions.
appendix_slides.answers_question: What happened to jobs? Did CBAM cause 11,000 job losses? Which other sectors are hurt? Are the negatives only downstream? What would you study next?

appendix_slides.title: A13. Company-case fine print: did CBAM force these contracts?
appendix_slides.content: Dates against policy dates: CBAM proposed 14 Jul 2021; reporting from 1 Oct 2023; definitive 1 Jan 2026 [S3][S7][S6]. Volvo Group x SSAB fossil-free steel load carrier, 13 Oct 2021 (after the proposal, before reporting; Volvo Group, not Volvo Cars) [U17]. BMW, 20 Oct 2021: agreement to source hydrogen or renewable-power steel, first deliveries originally from 2025, up to 95% lower production emissions; not all BMW steel [U15]. Mercedes-Benz x Stegra, Jun 2023, about 50,000 t/yr; Mercedes is buyer, Stegra producer [U14]. VW x Thyssenkrupp MoU, 22 Oct 2024 (during reporting): commissioning from 2027 (gas first), supply from 2028 [U10]; the notes' 'full hydrogen operation by 2029' for a 2.5 Mt/yr Duisburg plant is a different statement, reconcile before quoting both. Salzgitter x EWE, 9 Jun 2026 (after the definitive start): 10,000 t/yr, 7 years, about 6.5% of SALCOS need [U13]. Stegra review 30 Sep 2026: more capital needed [U16]. bluemint is a product family; bluemint recycled uses processed scrap in the blast furnace [U11]. Outokumpu: 97% recycled material content in 2025, a recycling route; stainless is not interchangeable with automotive flat carbon steel [U18]. Finland-to-Germany steel is intra-EU: no new CBAM border charge, which is different from a zero footprint [U4].
